summary: Describes how an EPP session maps onto a single TCP connection, with required use of TLS to protect exchanged information. It obsoletes RFC 3734. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 5734.

plainLanguage.summary: This note says how the registry language travels over a locked internet connection.

questions: how does epp work over tcp
how does epp frame messages on tcp
subtitle: How EPP sessions travel over TCP connections with encryption

tldr.problem: EPP needs a reliable transport mechanism that can deliver XML commands and responses between registrars and registries, with strong encryption to protect credentials and sensitive registry operations.
tldr.mechanism: EPP over TCP maps EPP sessions to single TCP connections, requiring TLS (Transport Layer Security) encryption for confidentiality and mutual authentication. Messages are framed with a 32-bit length header followed by XML payload.
tldr.outcome: Registry operators and registrars can securely communicate using a standard transport that works with existing internet infrastructure. RFC 4934 replaced RFC 3734 with minor updates to security and operational descriptions.

today: RFC 4934 is a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 5734 with similar minor updates and clarifications. The core concepts of mapping EPP to TCP and TLS remain standard and widely deployed in domain registry infrastructure.

sections.title: Mapping EPP to TCP and TLS
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is a framework for managing provisioning of internet resources like domain names. By itself, EPP defines the structure and semantics of commands and responses in XML, but not how those messages are transmitted. This RFC specifies how to map EPP sessions onto single TCP connections using TLS for security.

EPP over TCP is straightforward: one EPP session corresponds to one TCP connection. The client initiates an OPEN call to a listening server on TCP port 700 (assigned by IANA). After TCP connection establishment, the server sends an EPP <greeting> message. The client then logs in with <login>, exchanges commands and responses, and closes the session with <logout>.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP over TCP means one client connects to one server using a single TCP line, and they stay connected for the whole conversation. The registry listens on port 700 for connections.

sections.title: Session Establishment and Lifecycle
sections.content:
A client establishes an EPP session by issuing an active OPEN call to the server's TCP port. After the TCP three-way handshake completes, the server MUST send an EPP <greeting> containing the server's name, version, and supported mechanisms. This greeting tells the client what the server can do.

The session is normally ended by the client issuing an EPP <logout> command, after which the server closes the TCP connection. Servers MAY limit connection lifetime to prevent resource exhaustion—they can close idle connections after a server-defined timeout, or close long-lived active connections. A client MAY also end the session by directly closing the TCP connection, though this is less graceful than a proper logout.

Important: A single EPP session MUST be confined to a single TCP connection. Clients cannot pipeline commands across multiple connections. However, clients MAY establish multiple TCP connections to support multiple simultaneous EPP sessions with the same server.
sections.plainLanguage: To start, the client opens a TCP line to port 700. The server says hello with a greeting. Then they can talk until the client says goodbye with a logout. If no one talks for too long, the server closes the line.

sections.title: Command-Response Exchange and Message Ordering
sections.content:
EPP follows a command-response paradigm: after authentication, the client sends commands and the server returns responses, all on the same TCP connection. Every EPP command results in exactly one EPP response. Commands MUST be processed independently and in the same order they are sent from the client.

Although TCP allows pipelining (sending multiple commands before the first response arrives), EPP commands are idempotent—processing a command twice has the same net effect as processing it once. This means if the TCP connection closes after the server processes a command but before sending the response, the server MAY undo the command's effects to ensure consistency.

Servers SHOULD impose a time limit for clients to issue well-formed EPP commands. If a well-formed command is not received within the limit, the server SHOULD end the session and close the connection. This prevents clients from hanging idle indefinitely while holding server resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends one command, the server sends back one answer. If the connection breaks right after the server finishes a command, the server can undo it to keep everything in sync. Clients who don't send commands for a while get disconnected.

sections.title: Data Unit Format and Framing
sections.content:
EPP data units are framed to delimit individual messages. Each data unit consists of two parts: a 32-bit header (in network byte order, big-endian) specifying the total length of the data unit in octets (including the header itself), followed by the EPP XML instance.

The receiver reads the 32-bit length, then reads that many additional octets to obtain the complete EPP XML message. This explicit framing allows the receiver to determine where one EPP message ends and the next begins without parsing XML, which is important for stream-oriented protocols like TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message starts with a 4-byte number saying 'this message is N bytes long', then the XML comes next. The receiver reads the number first, so it knows exactly how much data to read before the next message starts.

sections.title: TLS Security and Mutual Authentication
sections.content:
EPP's base protocol provides only simple username and password authentication, which offers no protection against passive attacks. To protect EPP over TCP, TLS version 1.0 or later MUST be used. Using the latest TLS version supported by both parties provides confidentiality, integrity, and mutual authentication of client and server machines.

Mutual authentication using the TLS Handshake Protocol is REQUIRED. Both client and server MUST validate the complete certification path, including signature validity, validity periods, and machine names. EPP service MUST NOT be granted until the TLS handshake completes successfully and both certificates are validated.

After TLS establishes the secure channel, EPP sends a second-level authentication: the EPP <login> command with a client identifier and password. This supplements the machine-level TLS authentication, allowing multiple user identities per client machine.

Servers are vulnerable to TCP-based denial-of-service attacks (e.g., SYN floods). Operators SHOULD deploy firewalls and router filters to restrict inbound server access to known, trusted clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any EPP login happens, TLS creates a locked channel where both sides check each other's certificates to make sure they're trustworthy. Then EPP adds a username and password login on top of that. This double-layer security keeps the connection safe.
